```{r load-packages, include = FALSE}
# Add any additional packages you need to this chunk
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(knitr)

```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# For better figure resolution
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.retina = 3, dpi = 300, fig.width = 6, fig.asp = 0.618, out.width = "80%")
```

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# Load your data here
# Supply column names because the original temperature headers contain degree symbols.
bikes <- read_csv(
  "data/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  skip = 1,
  col_names = c(
    "date", "rentals", "hour", "temperature_c", "humidity_pct",
    "wind_speed_ms", "visibility_10m", "dew_point_c", "solar_radiation",
    "rainfall_mm", "snowfall_cm", "season", "holiday", "functioning"
  ),
  col_types = cols(date = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y"))
)

# Compare rental counts only during hours when the service was operating.
bikes_open <- bikes %>%
  filter(functioning == "Yes") %>%
  mutate(
    weekday = wday(date),
    # Sunday is 1 and Saturday is 7. Public holidays also count as non-working days.
    day_type = if_else(
      weekday == 1 | weekday == 7 | holiday == "Holiday",
      "Non-working day",
      "Working day"
    )
  )

# Each group gives one point on a curve. Keep the number of observations behind each mean.
hourly_rentals <- bikes_open %>%
  group_by(season, day_type, hour) %>%
  summarise(
    n_hours = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(rentals)
  )
```

class: center, middle

## How do mean hourly bike rentals differ between working days and non-working days in Seoul across the four seasons?

---

# Which hours did we compare?

We used hourly rental counts from the Seoul Bike Sharing Demand dataset, covering 1 December 2017 to 30 November 2018. The service was operating during 8,465 of the 8,760 recorded hours.

| Day type | Days included | Operating hours |
|:---------|:--------------|----------------:|
| Working day | Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays | 5,712 |
| Non-working day | Weekends and public holidays | 2,753 |

Each point on a curve shows the mean number of rentals for that season, day type and hour of day.

Source: [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5F62R)

---

# Hourly rentals by season and day type

```{r slide-hourly-rentals, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.asp=0.48, out.width="85%"}
# Keep the same vertical scale across all four seasons.
ggplot(
  data = hourly_rentals,
  mapping = aes(x = hour, y = mean_rentals, colour = day_type)
) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ season, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean rentals per hour",
    colour = "Day type"
  )
```

---

# Peak times and the gap at 08:00

| Season | Working-day peak | Non-working-day peak | Extra rentals on working days at 08:00 |
|:-------|:----------------:|:--------------------:|---------------------------------------:|
| Spring | 18:00 | 17:00 | 920 |
| Summer | 18:00 | 20:00 | 1,100 |
| Autumn | 18:00 | 17:00 | 1,227 |
| Winter | 08:00 | 15:00 | 442 |

We chose 08:00 for a closer look because the largest positive gap occurred at 08:00 in each of the four seasons.

---

# Does the working-day gap at 08:00 vary by season?

We compared two linear models using the 353 mornings with rental data at 08:00.

| Model | Working-day gap at 08:00 | Adjusted R² |
|:------|:-------------------------|------------:|
| Common-gap model | One gap shared by all four seasons | 0.5973 |
| Seasonal-gap model | A separate gap for each season | 0.6296 |

Allowing the gap to vary by season increased adjusted R² by about 0.032. This indicates a better fit to the observed mornings.

---

# How much do rentals vary at 08:00?

```{r slide-morning-residuals, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.asp=0.45, out.width="85%"}
# Fit the seasonal-gap model to one observation per operating morning.
morning <- bikes_open %>%
  filter(hour == 8)

seasonal_gap <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(rentals ~ season * day_type, data = morning)

# Compare observed rentals with the fitted value for each morning.
morning_check <- morning %>%
  bind_cols(predict(seasonal_gap, morning)) %>%
  mutate(residual = rentals - .pred)

ggplot(morning_check, aes(x = day_type, y = residual)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ season, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Observed minus fitted rentals at 08:00")
```

At 08:00, the residual standard deviation was larger on working days in all four seasons. In spring, it was about 656 rentals per hour on working days and 247 on non-working days.

---

# Conclusions and limitations

- On working days, mean rentals peaked at 18:00 in spring, summer and autumn, and at 08:00 in winter.
- On non-working days, the peak came at 15:00 in winter, 17:00 in spring and autumn, and 20:00 in summer.
- In every season, the largest gap between working and non-working days occurred at 08:00. Working days averaged 442 more rentals at that hour in winter and 1,227 more in autumn.

**Limitation:** The data cover one year in Seoul. A second year would help us check whether these peak times and morning gaps recur.
